papers.title: Predictive Grid Cell Coding Does Not Require Explicit Planning
papers.abstract: Predictive grid cells, a recently discovered functional class of neurons in medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), exhibit grid-like tuning, not with respect to where an animal currently is, but where it will be. Such coding, which is disjoint from standard grid cell coding, appears consistent with the hypothesis that MEC supports predictive computations for goal-directed navigation. However, given that existing predictive coding theories have been used to understand standard grid cells, it remains unclear what the functional significance of predictive grid cells is. Furthermore, the extent to which predictive grid cells are generally present in MEC is unknown. To address these open questions, we analyze data from rodent electrophysiology recordings and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In an independent, previously recorded MEC dataset, we find evidence of predictive grid cell coding when the animal is awake and exploring an open field environment, suggesting that they are a general feature of rodent MEC. In RNNs trained to path-integrate, which have previously been shown to develop units with grid-like representations, we also find units with predictive grid-like representations, even though the RNNs are not trained with a predictive objective. We validate the predictive grid tuning of these units by finding that they exhibit significant future path-dependence, even when controlling for the same allocentric spatial position. In addition, we find that band-like units, which have been found to play an important role in maintaining path-integration in the RNNs, exhibit greater predictive grid tuning than expected by chance. These results lead us to hypothesize that predictive grid cells are a property of the underlying grid cell circuit. We test this by looking for signatures of predictive grid coding in the MEC electrophysiological data collected during sleep, finding evidence in one recording. Collectively, our results challenge the idea that predictive grid cells must necessarily be used for explicit prediction and planning, and instead may be involved in shaping the population level activity of grid cells.

papers.title: Aging effects on retrospective and naturalistic encoding of time and their relationship with memory.
papers.abstract: In everyday life, attention is not explicitly directed toward time. Yet, we can reconstruct how long an experience lasted from the memory traces it left behind, a process intertwined with episodic memory and subjective experience. As both memory and temporal processing change with advancing age, investigating aging effects could provide critical insights on these reconstructive processes. In this study, 31 younger (aged 24{+/-}3) and 36 older (aged 69{+/-}6) healthy adults completed two EEG sessions: 1) a resting-state recording followed by an unexpected retrospective time estimation, and 2) a video-based prospective duration estimation task where participants encoded and judged the duration of 50 naturalistic videos (2-32s) varying in eventfulness. Using a cycle-by-cycle burst analysis of alpha (: 8-12 Hz), we examined oscillatory correlates of both retrospective temporal judgement and prospective temporal processing. Behaviorally, both groups reconstructed short intervals similarly, but older adults produced longer prospective duration estimates than younger adults for longer video clips (16-32s), particularly under low-eventfulness. Regression analyses also showed that individual differences in older adults' prospective duration judgments were influenced by both their retrospective time estimation and episodic memory abilities, especially for longer videos. At the neural level, resting-state -burst dynamics were higher in older adults and predicted, with -power, longer retrospective estimates in older adults. Additionally, resting-state -burst activity predicted -burst during video encoding in both groups. Together, these findings reveal that individual -power and -burst dynamics could constitute memory-based time-tracking mechanism that aging reshapes in ways that manifest behaviorally under naturalistic conditions.

papers.title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder
papers.abstract: Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia (VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNF/NF-{kappa}B (IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways (STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR), complement activation (CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3), extracellular matrix remodeling (COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2), and unfolded protein response (BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.

papers.title: Disease progression shapes circadian and locomotor disruption in a model of multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system featuring a wide range of debilitating symptoms. Wearable activity recording devices have recently been adopted to improve symptom monitoring in MS, capturing symptoms related to sleep/wake cycles, circadian disruption, and fatigue. However, comparable measures of activity have yet been established in pre-clinical models of MS, the most widely used being experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We therefore sought to characterize changes in continual home-cage activity over the course of EAE, and establish whether home-cage monitoring can be used as an observer-independent measure of disease progression. Our results showed that locomotor activity in the mid-active/dark phase was most severely affected by EAE. Disrupted circadian (24-hour) activity was observed during the peak and onset stages of disease. Bout activity analysis revealed >40-minute long activity bouts as a sensitive indicator of non-motor symptoms independent of clinical score-based motor deficits. Current assessment of disease progression in EAE relies on clinical scores, which primarily assess motor deficits through visual observation prone to observer bias. Various computed activity parameters were found to be altered during key disease stages, suggesting that a combination of activity measures can serve as objective indicators of disease progression. Overall, our results show that home-cage activity effectively captures signs of non-motor symptoms in the EAE model of MS and can serve as an observer-independent measure of EAE disease progression.

papers.title: Agency and Embodiment Provide Dissociable Benefits to Perception, Metacognition and Neural Processing During Active Sensing
papers.abstract: Metacognition, judging how reliable our own perceptual decisions are, is central to adaptive behavior. Such judgments hinge on the reliability of the sensory evidence on which that decision is based, and active sensing through self-directed exploration is known to improve perception itself. Yet, how agency, the authorship over self-initiated actions, and the processing of the sensory consequences, which is implicit to active sensing, modulate metacognition and its calibration, remains unknown. Whether physical embodiment adds to this beyond virtual exploration is similarly unclear, yet relevant both for daily life and for self-monitoring in agentic AI. Here, we combined a naturalistic auditory search paradigm with mobile electroencephalography. Twenty participants performed a target-detection task under three conditions: active embodied exploration , active screen-based exploration, and passive listening to replays of their own trials, while we obtained steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs) to characterize stimulus-locked neural responses. We find that both agency conditions improved accuracy, metacognitive sensitivity, and overall SSAEP amplitude relative to passive listening, indicating that agency, rather than whole-body movement, drives these enhancements. Crucially, however, embodiment uniquely grounded both the target-evoked neural response and the subjects' confidence to immediate sensory evidence. Thus, agency alone broadly enhances perceptual and neural processing, but embodiment specifically anchors confidence, neurally and behaviorally, to the present.

papers.title: Coupled neuro-fluid dynamics in human bioelectromagnetism
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) are widely interpreted as direct, non-invasive measures of neural population activity, assuming surrounding tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) act as passive volume conductors that distorts but do not contribute to signal generation. Using conductive-fluid phantom experiments, structural magnetic resonance imaging, and in vivo EEG and MEG recordings, the present report challenges this assumption. Mechanically driven conductive fluid generated structured, oscillatory, source-localizable electromagnetic signals resembling M/EEG in the absence of neural tissue, and interindividual differences in CSF volume systematically moderated M/EEG signal amplitude. These findings suggest that, at the scales accessed by invasive and non-invasive electrophysiology, electromagnetic and mechanical processes form a coupled system in which contributions of neural currents and fluid motion cannot readily be uniquely separated.

papers.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Circadian Phase Inference Methods for Bulk Transcriptomic Data
papers.abstract: Circadian phase can be inferred from gene expression when sample collection times are unavailable, but the available methods have not been systematically compared. We compared ten unsupervised phase inference methods and two clock-gene baselines on 25 datasets with reference times (16 real datasets from five studies and 9 simulations). The primary measure was the aligned circular mean absolute error (MAE), with a permutation test for significance, circular correlations and gene-level reconstruction of rhythmicity, acrophase and amplitude were secondary outcomes. CHIRAL had the lowest mean MAE (1.80 h, 95% confidence interval 1.21-2.97 h from resampling study families). The two clock-gene baselines (2.15 and 2.20 h) were next, followed by TEMPO, CYCLOPS and CYCLOPS 2.0 (2.49-2.80 h), and the confidence intervals of these six overlapped substantially. The other six methods had mean errors of 3.91-4.86 h, compared with 5.08-5.23 h for permuted phases. Accuracy depended on the dataset and on the strength of clock-gene rhythms, and, for several methods, on the random seed and the adjustment for batch or covariates. When the inferred phases were used to analyse gene rhythms in 22 datasets, the four leading methods identified rhythmic genes with a median ROC AUC of 0.64-0.70 and recovered gene acrophases with a median error of 0.18-0.64 h. In two mouse datasets without collection times, agreement with external reference acrophases differed between methods and tissues.

papers.title: Neocortical Feedback Biases Hippocampal Reactivation Toward Unconsolidated Memories in a Predictive-Coding Model of Systems Consolidation
papers.abstract: During sleep and quiet wakefulness, the brain spontaneously revisits neural activity patterns associated with previous experience, a phenomenon known as reactivation, or replay. Reactivation is thought to support systems consolidation, the process by which memory retrieval becomes progressively more dependent on neocortical circuits and less dependent on the hippocampus. Importantly, reactivation is not indiscriminate: it preferentially targets specific memories, such as new or weakly learned ones. These observations have motivated the development of computational models accounting for the spontaneous reactivation of memories, their prioritisation for replay, and their transfer between the hippocampus and neocortex. In parallel, predictive-coding (PC) models have shown how computations attributed to hippocampal and neocortical circuits can arise from local prediction-error dynamics. Here, we connect these two lines of work by showing how autonomous intrinsic dynamics in coupled PC networks can transfer stored memory content between neural systems. The hippocampus and neocortex are modelled as two coupled PC associative memory networks, with asymmetric coupling motivated by reported interactions between hippocampal area CA1 and the prefrontal cortex. This coupling establishes a closed-loop dialogue in which hippocampal activity drives neocortical learning, while neocortical feedback biases subsequent hippocampal activity toward content for which neocortical support remains weak. We prove that this feedback steers hippocampal activity toward states of higher neocortical free energy, so that prioritisation emerges from the dynamics rather than from an explicit scheduler. In our model, neocortical learning relies exclusively on spontaneous hippocampal activity, without access to the initial training corpus. Nevertheless, we show that the neocortical network acquires correlated memory content faster than direct training on randomly sampled memories. This advantage appeared for sufficiently correlated memories, grew with their correlation, and persisted when new memories were incrementally added during transfer. Together, these results provide a PC account in which neocortical feedback organises hippocampal reactivation to support efficient memory transfer during systems consolidation.

papers.title: A reinforcement learning framework for goal-directed stimulation of engineered neuronal networks
papers.abstract: Systematically perturbing neuronal circuits under controlled conditions offers a promising route to understanding how they encode and process information, yet remains methodologically demanding. In vitro neuronal networks can be cultured on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) that allow stimulation and recording, and microfluidic patterning can constrain network topology to yield stable stimulation-evoked responses. Yet, the space of possible spatiotemporal stimulation patterns remains too large for exhaustive exploration. Additionally, the evoked responses depend on prior stimulation history. Here, we present an open-source framework that sustains closed-loop reinforcement-learning (RL) control of engineered neuronal networks, sending electrical stimuli to the MEA and evaluating the evoked responses to identify stimulation patterns that drive specific target activity motifs. We extend inkube, a low-cost, open-source electrophysiology system from off-the-shelf components, with closed-loop electrophysiology. This enables reliable delivery of stimulation at single-sample precision with millisecond-range round-trip times. It also allows independent RL agents to control multiple networks simultaneously. As a proof-of-principle application, we benchmarked different agents on the task of identifying stimulation patterns that maximise the length of clockwise-circular firing sequences. We first demonstrated that stimulation-evoked responses in engineered recurrent networks were stable and separable across the action space over hours of continuous operation. We characterised the dependency of responses on prior stimulation history, finding state dependence in a subset of stimulus pairs. The agents learned to improve reward during training with respect to random stimulation. Agents converged on non-trivial stimulation patterns that span the full action space rather than mirroring the target motif. All hardware designs and software are publicly available, providing an accessible platform for goal-directed functional characterisation of engineered neuronal networks at single-spike resolution.

papers.title: Discovery of GluA3 preferring AMPA receptor positive allosteric modulator BRD3290
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is a debilitating neuropsychiatric disease that lacks effective treatments for many symptom domains including negative, cognitive and sleep disturbances. Lack of clear disease etiology has hampered the development of new, effective treatments for the unmet needs of people with schizophrenia. Large scale human genetics have identified rare loss of function mutations that substantially increase risk of developing schizophrenia, including in GRIA3, the gene that encodes the GluA3 receptor subunit of the AMPA receptor (AMPAR). Several drug discovery programs have been aimed at developing AMPAR positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) as a novel treatment for schizophrenia. Despite intense drug discovery efforts, there are no FDA approved AMPAR PAMs. We therefore hypothesized that selectively targeting GluA3, the AMPAR subunit implicated by human genetics, could yield a safer and more effective AMPAR PAM for the potential treatment of schizophrenia. Using a combination of medicinal chemistry, in vitro, and in vivo studies, we discovered BRD3290, a GluA3-preferring AMPAR PAM with reasonable potency in heterologous cells, as well as favorable tolerability and brain exposure. Peripheral administration of BRD3290 engaged an established AMPAR PAM target engagement biomarker but did not improve performance of wildtype mice in the novel object recognition task (NOR), in contrast to the nonselective AMPAR PAM PF-4778574, which improved mouse NOR. These findings suggest that the GluA3 selectivity profile of BRD3290 was insufficient to enhance cognitive function in this mouse NOR paradigm. This work highlights the challenges of AMPAR subtype-selective modulation and provides molecular insights into the ability to develop subtype-selective AMPAR PAMs.

papers.title: Cross-species multi-omics integration reveals lung alterations in acute kidney injury across mouse, pig, and human airway organoid models
papers.abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently associated with the development of distant acute lung injury (ALI); however, its broader clinical impact and the underlying temporal molecular mechanics remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We used aggregate deidentified Epic Cosmos data to describe all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay (LOS) in an AKI cohort (13,815,092 patients; 2016-2025) and a subgroup with subsequent lung injury (AKI-lung). Mechanistically, we integrated matched RNA-seq and proteomics from a hyper-acute pig model (4 h reperfusion), an established mouse model (24 h reperfusion), and primary lung organoids exposed to mtDAMP-conditioned media, using MOFA+, PROGENy, decoupleR/CollecTRI, and DIABLO. Candidates were validated in primary human donor lungs obtained from LifeLink, separated into Control (< 1.3 mg/dL, n = 4) and Clinical AKI ([≥] 1.3 mg/dL, n = 3) groups based on admission blood creatinine level. Results: The AKI-lung subgroup had higher observed mortality than the overall AKI cohort (36.67% vs. 25.45%, p < 0.001). Mean hospital LOS was 11.3 versus 6.9 days in the reported AKI-lung and AKI alone queries, respectively (unadjusted p < 0.001). Multi-omics analyses cross-species indicated a temporal shift in proteogenomic coupling. In the hyper-acute pig model, we observed a largely post-translational response (r = -0.06), including ciliary breakdown and metabolic changes associated with PDHA1 protein depletion (Log2FC = -1.53), with minimal transcript level changes. The established mouse model showed a coordinated transcriptional inflammatory response (r = 0.316), characterized by PI3K/Akt pathway activation and downregulation of vascular and immune regulators (Aplnr, Cd74). Human lung organoids exhibited transcriptional downregulation of tissue remodeling genes and persistent ATF6/ATF4-associated ER stress, consistent with a reparative phase under proteostatic strain. Unsupervised MOFA+ revealed conserved cross-species axes (Factors 6 and 7) linked to vascular repair and hemostasis. Upstream regulon analysis identified the endothelial integrity regulators, including FOXF1. Most importantly, targeted validation in primary human donor lungs confirmed a statistically significant, selective down-regulation of the core circadian regulator circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) transcript (p < 0.05), independent of donor age, sex, race. Conclusions: Aggregate clinical findings suggest an association between lung injury following AKI and worse outcome. Kidney-Lung crosstalk initiates as hyper-acute post-translational microvascular breakdown in swine and rapidly transitions into localized uncoupling of cell-autonomous pulmonary circadian machinery (CLOCK) in clinical human AKI, offering human-validated targets to intercept distant organ failure.

papers.title: Agreement between Garmin and Ultrahuman wearables and their association with continuous glucose monitoring: an n-of-1 study
papers.abstract: Background: Consumer wearables and continuous glucose monitors (CGM) are increasingly worn together outside clinical settings. Few studies have examined whether two wearables worn at the same time agree with each other, and whether either tracks glucose metrics derived from CGM. Objective: In one adult under free-living conditions, we examined (1) how well sleep, heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV) and activity metrics from a Garmin smartwatch and an Ultrahuman ring agreed with each other, and (2) how these metrics related to glucose measured by CGM. Methods: One healthy adult with no diagnosed diabetes wore a Garmin Fenix 8 watch on the wrist, an Ultrahuman Ring AIR and an Abbott FreeStyle Libre CGM at the same time for 12 days (29 July to 9 August 2026; 1101 glucose readings). We assessed agreement between the devices with Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis (mean bias and 95% limits of agreement, LoA) for daily metrics and for heart rate within the day, and with Cohen's kappa for sleep stages, minute by minute. We related the wearable metrics to mean glucose, glucose variability (coefficient of variation, CV%) and time in range (TIR, 3.9 to 10.0 mmol/L), reading by reading (over the whole record and separately for sleep and waking hours) and day by day. All correlations are descriptive. Because the Ultrahuman ring recorded no data for 22 hours on 3 August and its daytime heart rate behaved differently afterwards, heart-rate analyses are reported for the whole period and separately before and after that gap. The daily results were checked by leaving out one day at a time and by excluding the first 24 hours of sensor wear. Results: The devices agreed closely on total sleep duration (r=0.94; bias -0.02 h, 95% LoA -0.56 to 0.51 h). Daily steps correlated strongly (r=0.99 over the 11 days with data from both devices), but Garmin counted more steps on every day (mean 11,157 vs. 8,929 steps per day; bias +2228 steps). Heart rate agreed moderately during sleep (r=0.68). While awake, agreement was moderate before the gap (r=0.54) and absent after it (r=0.08), when Ultrahuman's daytime heart rate stayed near 70 bpm. The devices assigned the same sleep stage in 50.0% of 4525 minutes (kappa=0.28). Mean glucose was 5.13 mmol/L (SD 0.82) and TIR was 97.5%. Of all wearable signals, heart rate was most closely associated with glucose (Garmin r=0.43 over all readings), but the correlation fell to 0.34 within sleep and 0.21 within waking hours, and before the gap the two devices' waking correlations were alike (Garmin 0.25, Ultrahuman 0.24). Across the 12 days, correlations between night-time wearable metrics and glucose variability weakened markedly when the first 24 hours of sensor wear were excluded (absolute r fell from 0.59 or more to 0.34 or less), and TIR was 100% on 8 of the 12 days, which left it little room to vary. Conclusions: The two wearables agreed on how long the participant slept but not on how the night was staged, and their heart-rate agreement depended on whether the participant was asleep or awake and on the period of wear. Of all wearable signals, heart rate was most closely associated with glucose, mainly because both are lower at night and higher during the day. The associations across days rested largely on the first night of sensor wear. In this single participant, the devices behaved differently by device and by period of wear, so studies that combine different wearables, or relate them to CGM, should check for such differences before pooling data.

papers.title: Context Shapes Alpha-Band Electrophysiological Signatures Under Psilocybin
papers.abstract: Background: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic that provides a pharmacological tool for examining neural activity associated with altered states of consciousness. Existing studies report reduced power (4-30 Hz) in posterior regions and altered functional connectivity (FC) at rest, but have typically involved small samples and coarse anatomical parcellations. Additionally, perceptual engagement has been shown to attenuate psilocybin-related whole-brain FC changes. However, how naturalistic context modifies psilocybin's frequency-specific electrophysiological effects remains incompletely characterised. Methods: We analysed the largest psilocybin electroencephalography (EEG) dataset to date (n = 56), with matched baseline recordings acquired before psilocybin administration. EEG was recorded during movie viewing, eyes-closed rest, guided meditation, and music listening. Cortical source activity was estimated using minimum-norm estimation and analysed across six canonical frequency bands (1-80 Hz). Spectral power, alpha peak frequency (APF), and magnitude-squared coherence within and between seven functional networks were quantified. Psilocybin effects were assessed using permutation testing with FDR correction, and linear mixed-effects models separated the contributions of drug, context, and their interaction to alpha-band connectivity. Results: At rest, psilocybin decreased alpha (8-13 Hz) power, increased gamma-range power, and elevated APF. Alpha-band FC decreased within and between higher-order networks implicated in top-down control. Relative to eyes-closed rest, psilocybin-context interactions showed that structured sensory environments attenuated or reversed psilocybin-related alpha-band connectivity changes. Conclusions: These findings identify alpha-band activity as a key electrophysiological correlate of psilocybin-related changes in cortical communication. Structured sensory input reshapes psilocybin-related cortical dynamics, particularly alpha-band connectivity across large-scale cortical networks, with the strength and direction of this modulation differing by context.

papers.title: Modulating Sleep Oscillations Through Targeted Memory Reactivation: Linking Functional Dynamics to Brain Microstructure
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation reputedly rely on the coordinated activity of sleep oscillations, which may facilitate the reactivation and redistribution of newly acquired memories. Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during sleep can experimentally modulate these processes, although effects remain variable. Moreover, how learning-related microstructural plasticity relates to sleep oscillatory activity and spindle-related network dynamics remains poorly understood. We investigated whether auditory TMR modulates sleep spindles, slow oscillations (SOs) and their co-occurrence, whether these changes relate to motor memory consolidation and diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures of brain microstructure, and whether learning and TMR alter the evolution of cortico-cortical connectivity during spindle development. Methods: Sixty healthy young adults underwent five dMRI sessions before and after motor sequence learning (Day 1), after a post-training night of regular sleep (RS) or TMR (Day 2), and before and after relearning (Day 5). Baseline and experimental nights were recorded with 256-channel high-density EEG. Oscillation densities were analyzed using mixed-design ANOVAs and related to behavioral and dMRI changes using Pearson or Spearman correlations. Intra-spindle connectivity between 148 source-reconstructed cortical regions was compared between spindle onset and end, across nights and between groups using Network-Based Statistics. Results: Spindle density, SO density and SO-spindle co-occurrence remained stable across nights in the RS group but decreased after TMR. Higher spindle density and co-occurrence were associated with greater overnight performance gains, and all oscillatory measures were associated with learning-related dMRI changes in subcortical regions, notably striatum and thalamus. Connectivity increased from the beginning to the end of the spindle duration during the baseline night in both groups, but during the experimental night only in the RS group. Conclusions: Motor learning is associated with coordinated changes in sleep oscillatory activity, within-spindle cortical connectivity and brain microstructure, supporting a dynamic interaction between learning-induced plasticity and sleep-dependent network reorganization. Under the present stimulation conditions, TMR did not enhance these processes but instead reduced sleep oscillatory activity and attenuated spindle-related connectivity dynamics, underscoring the importance of precisely targeting endogenous sleep rhythms when using TMR.

papers.title: How variable and stress-sensitive is sleep expression in lizards?
papers.abstract: Sleep expression in wild animals is regulated by ecological context. Yet, how sleep differs between populations of a species that experience different environmental challenges such as urbanization, remains to be fully understood. Robust quantification of sleep in small animals, such as lizards, has so far been methodologically difficult, limiting population-level comparisons. Using recently developed miniature loggers, we recorded sleep in 19 wild-caught individuals of the South Indian rock agama lizard (Psammophilus dorsalis). We compared individuals captured from urban and rural environments and measured electro-oculogram (EOG)-derived sleep parameters: sleep duration, bout frequency, bout duration, and interval between bouts. We then subjected all individuals to an acute stressor (handling-restraint) and examined changes in sleep expression. We found that this species slept mostly at night, with an average total sleep time of 11h 10min. EOG-derived sleep characteristics did not differ substantially between populations, although daytime sleep bouts were more consolidated (shorter interval between bouts) in urban-origin lizards. Contrary to evidence from mammals, acute restraint stress did not impact sleep, overall or for either population. To complement these measures, we also quantified the latency to arousal after exposure to vibration stimuli in a separate set of urban and rural lizards (n = 12 each) and found that urban individuals responded marginally quicker at night compared to rural individuals, demonstrating greater vigilance and/or more fragmented sleep. Overall, we show that sleep characteristics of wild animals in a common garden can be highly conserved within a species, with limited context-dependent variation between populations.

papers.title: Retuning ventral hippocampal output improves social memory and reduces anxiety-related behavior in temporal lobe epilepsy
papers.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is associated with cognitive, social, and emotional comorbidities that persist between seizures and remain poorly addressed by seizure-focused treatment. We examined whether these interictal deficits reflect altered ventral CA1/subiculum (vCA1/Sub) output and whether shifting principal-cell excitability can improve behavior despite persistent pathology. In pilocarpine-treated mice, vCA1/Sub principal neurons were depolarized and showed altered recruitment, alveus/oriens stimulation produced diminished hyperpolarizing responses, and parvalbumin- and somatostatin-immunopositive cell densities were reduced in stratum oriens. Epileptic mice did not demonstrate social discrimination above chance despite retained social approach and social-odor preference and showed increased open-field center avoidance. Multiplexed chemogenetic inhibition of vCA1/Sub principal cells improved social discrimination and center exploration, whereas stronger inhibition did not reproduce the social-memory benefit. Within individual mice, discrimination was higher in predicted retuned than off-optimal states, and performance across inferred excitability states followed an inverted-U-like relationship. Anxiety-related and social improvements covaried across epileptic mice, consistent with shared dependence on vCA1/Sub circuit state. In a separate EEG cohort, moderate inhibition suppressed local hippocampal activity during the behavior-aligned interval without detectably reducing spontaneous seizures or early interictal spikes. These findings identify excessive vCA1/Sub output as a modifiable contributor to socio-affective dysfunction in TLE and show that retuning a disease-altered circuit can improve interictal behavior without acute seizure suppression.

papers.title: Relating layer fMRI signals to acoustics and intracranial neuronal activity in the human auditory cortex in a naturalistic design
papers.abstract: Naturalistic auditory perception engages feedforward and feedback dynamics across cortical depths, yet how these are organized in the human auditory cortex has been difficult to verify noninvasively. Here, we examine depth-dependent coupling between neuronal activity and fMRI during passive music listening. Depth-specific fMRI responses were modeled using neuronal oscillation envelopes elicited by the same naturalistic stimuli from a separate group of patients under intracranial EEG monitoring. From deep toward superficial depths, the relationship between oscillatory power and fMRI responses systematically changed: alpha/beta activity (8-30 Hz) was increasingly associated with negative fMRI responses, mapping top-down feedback, while gamma band (>30 Hz) oscillations showed increasingly positive associations. Relative to a purely acoustical fMRI baseline, broadband high-frequency activity (>70 Hz), a proxy for neuronal firing, showed the strongest coupling to BOLD signals at intermediate cortical depths receiving feedforward inputs from earlier auditory pathways. Our findings reveal a spectrolaminar organization of neurovascular coupling in the human auditory cortex.

papers.title: Vigilance profiles at sleep onset in patients with difficulty initiating sleep, with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: Difficulty initiating sleep (DIS) is a core insomnia complaint, frequently associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms, yet its objective correlates remain elusive. Insomnia subtypes were merged into a single diagnosis in DSM-5 and ICSD-3 because their criteria lacked reliability, leaving open whether objective markers could help characterize insomnia heterogeneity. Conventional polysomnography (PSG) reduces the wake-sleep transition to a single 30-s epoch. We combined conventional and continuous EEG-based vigilance markers to characterize sleep onset in patients with and without a DIS complaint, and in patients with DIS with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed PSG recordings from 2,952 sleep-clinic patients, grouped by the self-reported complaint of difficulty falling asleep (Insomnia Severity Index item 1 [≥] 2: DIS, n = 1,328; no DIS, n = 1,624). In unmedicated patients with DIS (n = 556), depressive (BDI-II [≥] 14) and anxiety (STAI-T [≥] 45) symptoms were assessed. Vigilance was quantified on 3-s epochs with an intrinsic Vigilance Score (iVS), a probability-of-wakefulness index calibrated on each participant's own scored night, alongside the theta/alpha ratio and micro-sleep detection, and on 30-s epochs with automated hypnodensities. Results: Patients with DIS showed a longer sleep latency and slightly higher vigilance markers during both wakefulness and sleep, whereas the duration of the SOP itself was only marginally different (median 11.5 min in both groups). Deep sleep also accumulated later across the night (hypnodensity). In wakefulness preceding sleep onset, higher vigilance coexisted with more frequent brief vigilance drops. Among patients with DIS, depressive symptoms were associated with a less wake-like sleep-onset period despite more severe insomnia complaints, a finding not explained by differences in wake amount and convergent with hypnodensity. Anxiety symptoms showed a similar but weaker, non-significant pattern. Conclusions: In patients complaining of difficulty initiating sleep, the delay lies mainly before the first sleep epoch: once it is reached, progression to consolidated sleep is only marginally delayed, although its vigilance content may differ. Continuous EEG markers detect such differences, which are not captured by sleep staging. The association of depressive symptoms with a less vigilant sleep onset, despite worse complaints, suggests that similar insomnia complaints may rest on partly different physiological substrates, and that continuous vigilance markers could help revisit insomnia heterogeneity.

papers.title: SCN1A haploinsufficiency disrupts neural progenitor networks and accelerates neurogenesis in human Dravet syndrome forebrain assembloids
papers.abstract: Dravet syndrome is a severe childhood neurological disorder caused mostly due to mutations in the sodium channel gene SCN1A. Although the disorder is widely attributed to dysfunction of inhibitory neurons, growing evidence suggests that disease mechanisms may begin much earlier during brain development. To investigate the developmental consequences of SCN1A haploinsufficiency, we generated patient-derived dorsal-ventral forebrain assembloids that model key features of human corticogenesis. We found that SCN1A was expressed in ventricular zone neural progenitors and that its reduced expression was associated with impaired growth, disrupted ventricular zone organization, and progressive depletion of progenitor populations. We further demonstrated reduced progenitor proliferation and self-renewal, accelerated cell-cycle exit, and premature neuronal differentiation, leading to increased production of excitatory neurons and enhanced network excitability. Single cell transcriptomic analyses revealed reduced cycling radial glial cells, accelerated progenitor maturation, and dysregulation of gap junction and calcium signaling pathways. Following these findings, we examined progenitor calcium activity and found that SCN1A haploinsufficiency disrupted coordinated functional network organization, resulting in reduced recurrent connectivity and fragmentation of functional cellular assemblies. These abnormalities occurred despite preserved intrinsic electrophysiological properties of individual progenitors, indicating a defect in population-level coordination rather than single cell electrophysiology. Together, our findings identify disrupted progenitor communication as an early developmental consequence of SCN1A haploinsufficiency and suggest that abnormalities within neural progenitor populations contribute to altered corticogenesis, excitatory neurogenesis, and circuit hyperexcitability in Dravet syndrome. This work expands current disease models beyond interneuron dysfunction and highlights the developing ventricular zone as a potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease
papers.abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder's eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold, so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90--0.96): after this representation collapse happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder's learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An easy task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11--26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

papers.title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
papers.abstract: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.

papers.title: Real-time noise cancellation for EEG monitoring and brain-computer interfaces
papers.abstract: Raw electroencephalography (EEG) data suffer from a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Effective real-time cleaning of EEG would improve the robustness of EEG monitoring, brain-computer interfaces, and brain-state-dependent stimulation applications in both laboratory and real-life environments. Here, we present a real-time source-estimate-utilizing noise-discarding algorithm (rtSOUND) for EEG noise suppression. We adapted the established offline SOUND algorithm for real-time use and implemented it into an open-source EEG-processing software. Instead of using conventional temporal filtering, SOUND operates the data with a spatial filter. This makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications, since each streamed data sample can be cleaned separately in near real-time. Unlike temporal filtering methods, SOUND does not make assumptions about the frequency content of noise and brain signals but assumes that the noise topographies differ from those generated by brain activity. With an EEG forward model, rtSOUND cross-validates the EEG time series and estimates the spatial distribution of noise, resulting in a data-cleaning linear spatial filter. Each streamed EEG sample is processed synchronously, and the filter is periodically updated in an asynchronous parallel process. The algorithm rapidly updates the spatial filter in response to changes in the data, ensuring that noise reduction is both immediate and accurately adapted to the current EEG state. rtSOUND was validated with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-EEG and resting-state EEG datasets measured from 25 healthy subjects. SNR of both TMS-evoked potentials and resting-state data consistently improved across various metrics. rtSOUND particularly benefitted channels with poor SNR, while retaining the waveforms in high-quality channels. The algorithm was fast enough to process data streamed at 5 kHz. rtSOUND improves the SNR of EEG in real time, providing a robust method to improve signal quality for brain-state-monitoring applications.

papers.title: Reach plans for grasping vs. placing objects evoke different neural dynamics within a shared cortico-cerebellar mechanism.
papers.abstract: Many reach studies treat grasping as the endpoint of a reach, but grasping often initiates a sequence of actions, ending with placing the object. Grasping and placing both require object-specific encoding, but placing has different computational demands, introduced by the intent, sensory feedback, and tolerance for spatial error when alignment is required. Recent neuroimaging work suggests that object placement shares similar cortico-cerebellar networks with grasp, with modest increases in network segregation and cerebellar activity. Here, we ask whether Grasp and Place are better distinguished by their spatiotemporal dynamics in both behaviour and scalp-recorded EEG activity. Using high-density EEG and motion tracking, 31 participants performed alternating Grasp/Place movements of a 3D object from/toward an oriented target/template. Place movements were initiated faster but executed more slowly and with greater endpoint-orientation precision than Grasp, indicating distinct control strategies. ERP and microstate analyses revealed that Grasp and Place shared a peri-movement polarity switch, from posterior negativity/frontal positivity during preparation to posterior positivity/frontal negativity during execution. This shared pattern was amplified during Place preparation and prolonged during Place execution, with stronger expression of preparatory medial frontal/cerebellar and execution-related posterior/cerebellar microstate dynamics. Finally, SVM decoding indicated that task-specific information was primarily encoded in low-frequency EEG activity (below 6 Hz). These results confirm that grasping and placing recruit similar cortico-cerebellar mechanisms, yet different spatiotemporal dynamics are employed to support the distinct computational demands of these behaviours.

papers.title: Progressive neurodegeneration of the locus coeruleus drives rapid eye movement sleep fragmentation
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common early features of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). AD progression is also characterized by early and substantial degeneration of the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC), beginning with tau pathology and progressing to major neuronal loss. Although LC degeneration and sleep disruption progress in parallel, whether LC degeneration causally contributes to sleep abnormalities, and which sleep changes are associated with this process, remain unresolved. Human studies are largely correlative, while existing rodent models poorly reproduce progressive LC degeneration. Here, we employed progressive Caspase-3 (Casp3)-mediated LC ablation, with longitudinal sleep and calcium fiber photometry to monitor LC activity across defined stages of degeneration in adult female DBH-Cre mice. Histological analysis demonstrated graded, time-dependent LC degeneration, yielding mild degeneration (~25% neuronal loss) by day 8 post Casp3 injection and moderate degeneration (~50% loss) by day 18. Relative to baseline and to control mice, LC degeneration led to REM sleep fragmentation, emerging already at the mild degeneration stage. By the moderate stage, total REM sleep during light hours had significantly increased, while EEG theta power during REM sleep progressively declined across all stages of degeneration. Degeneration also blunted state-dependent LC calcium activity, significantly reducing the contrast between wakefulness and REM signal. Together, these results establish Casp3-mediated ablation as a model of progressive LC neurodegeneration and identify REM fragmentation and blunted state-dependent LC activity as its early functional signatures, providing a platform for studying how degeneration of neuromodulatory systems shapes sleep in a neurodegenerative disease-like state.

papers.title: Gene expression dynamics through time reveal low pleiotropy genes underlying local adaptation in silver birch (Betula pendula)
papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying local adaptation in boreal trees is important for assessing their adaptive potential under climate change. The role of pleiotropy in polygenic local adaptation remains poorly understood. Here we studied growth and temporal transcriptomic responses to photoperiod in three photoperiod treatments in three populations of Betula pendula within a two-week time period to identify genes and co-expression networks underlying local adaptation and to estimate the level of pleiotropy in population specific gene expression. We used RNA sequencing to characterize the temporal transcriptomic responses which were analyzed with variance partitioning, differential gene expression and weighted co-expression network analyses. Photoperiod treatment and sampling time were the main drivers of gene expression variation both at the co-expression module and single gene level. The majority of circadian clock and flowering time genes exhibited striking similarity across populations. Nevertheless, we detected small but significant population effects in the temporal gene expression patterns which were concentrated on the periphery of the co-expression networks consistent with low pleiotropy effects. Our findings suggest that local adaptation to growing season length among populations exhibiting very low genetic differentiation along a latitudinal cline in B. pendula is likely polygenic and potentially governed through low pleiotropy genes.

papers.title: Astrocytic Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay regulates calcium signaling to support synapse function and influence anxiety-like behavior
papers.abstract: How astrocytes achieve their diverse roles in the brain at the molecular level is poorly understood. In this study, we leverage mouse models, electrophysiology, calcium imaging, behavioral assays, and bioinformatic approaches to demonstrate that astrocyte activity and astrocyte-mediated mouse behavior depends on the highly conserved and selective RNA turnover pathway-nonsense-mediated RNA decay (NMD). Conditional deletion of the core NMD gene, Upf2, in mature astrocytes leads to enhanced basal Ca2+ signaling coupled with synapse dysfunction and elevated anxiety-like behavior. Restoring basal Ca2+ signaling in NMD-deficient astrocytes shifted synaptic transmission and minimized anxiety-associated behavior. Molecular bioinformatic analysis identified specific NMD target transcripts in astrocytes as candidates influencing calcium signaling pathways and neuro-glia interactions that support brain function. Our study is the first to demonstrate specific roles for NMD in astrocytes.

papers.title: Neuroelectrophysiological correlates of extended cessation of consciousness in advanced meditators: A multimodal EEG and MEG study
papers.abstract: In some contemplative traditions, 'extended cessation' (EC) refers to a state of advanced meditation in which the meditator self-reports intentionally suppressing their own consciousness and re-emerging with a profound sense of clarity and equanimity. Here, we present the first electrophysiological study of EC, in which five meditators underwent concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recording. EC significantly increased high-frequency global coherence in all five of the participants, yet it did not consistently affect Lempel-Ziv complexity or power across participants. Our results provide preliminary evidence that the neural signatures of EC may be distinct from other states that are characterized by a loss of consciousness, including deep sleep and anesthesia. EC may not be simply 'switching off' consciousness but rather reorganizing the neural dynamics that underlie consciousness.

papers.title: Cognitive tests of pattern separation as sleep-sensitive measures in middle-aged and older adults: An exploratory study
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are considered both a dementia risk factor and symptom. The present research aimed to identify cognitive tests sensitive to objective sleep quantity or quality, focusing on tests designed to evaluate the earliest cognitive changes in dementia. We recruited adults who were 50 years or older and remotely monitored their sleep patterns for 7 consecutive days using wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries. On day 7, participants completed different cognitive tests; the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), the Prodromal Alzheimers and Mild Cognitive Impairment battery from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), taxing pattern separation, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The final sample included 34 participants (mean age: 65.56, SD: 9.57). There were significant correlations between objective sleep quantity and PVT and MST performance. MoCA scores were correlated with performance on CANTAB and MST. Objective sleep quantity predicted MST performance when controlling for age, sex, and education. Tests of pattern separation are sensitive to objective sleep quantity and early cognitive changes associated with dementia. The sensitivity of pattern separation tests to sleep should be evaluated in a larger study, aiming to identify suitable clinical trial outcome measures for sleep-promoting treatments in older adults.

papers.title: Tetradic Dynamics of Dyadic Sensorimotor Coordination: A Multiscale EEG Hyperscanning Study
papers.abstract: How do leader and follower roles shape the brain mechanisms that support coordinated action between people? This question has therapeutic relevance for conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, where the capacity for reciprocal social coordination is a defining vulnerability. Here, we propose a tetradic framework and examine sensorimotor coordination in 16 healthy adult pairs (15 included in EEG analyses) using dual-brain EEG hyperscanning and a 2x2 within-subject design crossing Role (Leader/Follower) and Condition (Mirroring/Matching). Mirroring required resonance with a partner's movement; Matching required its controlled transformation. This contrast was designed to dissociate automatic from controlled coordination. Behaviourally, Mirroring produced a robust Follower reaction-time advantage: pooling an independent behavioural-only cohort (combined N=64) revealed a smaller Leader advantage, consistent with role-dependent attention-inhibition gating. At the neural level, tonic power and significant phasic condition clusters were greater during Matching than Mirroring, while role-dependent phasic clusters suggested an anticipatory sequence around Leader responses and post-response gating and rebound around Follower responses. Information-theoretic decomposition identified Leader-weighted predictive information in frontal and posterior perceptual regions, Follower-specific adaptive information across frontoparietal and sensorimotor cortices, sparse Synergy in lateral occipital, fusiform, and paracentral cortices, and Redundancy linking pars opercularis and lateral occipital cortex. These findings characterize tetradic coordination within dyads as a multiscale, role-asymmetric architecture in which top-down predictive control and bottom-up adaptive regulation are functionally dissociable. The tetradic framework provides an organizing scaffold for this dissociation, and the role-specific signatures it reveals may offer candidate biomarkers for clinical populations in whom interpersonal coordination is disrupted.
